chunks.part: Part 9 Traffic Control For Bicycle Facilities
chunks.text: The definitions and terms shown in Items A through G below, which are found in the Society of Automotive Engineers standard SAE J3016 and other sources, are used extensively in automated vehicle technology. Their definitions, which are summarized below for reference and for use with the provisions of this Manual, are as follows: A. Advanced Driver Assistance Systems (ADAS) - Electronic systems that aid a vehicle driver with one or more driving tasks while driving. They are intended to increase the safe operation of a vehicle and include applications such as automatic braking, lane keeping assistance, adaptive cruise control, and others. B. Automated Driving System (ADS) - The hardware and software that are collectively capable of performing the entire Dynamic Driving Task (DDT) on a sustained basis, regardless of whether it is limited to a specific Operational Design Domain (ODD); this term is used specifically to describe a Level 3, 4, or 5 driving automation system. C. Automation Levels - The levels of automation that are described in Table 5A-1. D. Cooperative Automation - Technology that enables communication with other vehicles and the infrastructure to coordinate automated vehicle operation. E. Driving Automation System - The hardware and software that are collectively capable of performing part or all of the DDT on a sustained basis; this term is used generically to describe any system capable of Levels 1 through 5 driving automation. F. Dynamic Driving Task (DDT) - All of the real-time operational and tactical functions required to operate a vehicle in on-road traffic, excluding the strategic functions such as trip scheduling and selection of destinations and waypoints. G. Operational Design Domain (ODD) - Operating conditions under which a given driving automation system or feature thereof is specifically designed to function, including, but not limited to, environmental, geographical, and time-of-day restrictions, and/or the requisite presence or absence of certain traffic or roadway characteristics. Table 5A-1. Automation Levels Automation Level Description Automation Automation Category Type Level 0 The full-time performance by the human driver of all aspects of the Dynamic Driving Task, even when enhanced by warning or momentary intervention systems. None* None The driving mode specific execution by a sustained driver assistance system of either steering or acceleration/deceleration using information about the driving environment and with the expectation that the human driver performs all remaining aspects of the Dynamic Driving Task. Advanced Level 1 Driver Assistance Systems (ADAS) The driving mode specific execution by one or more sustained driver assistance systems of both steering and acceleration/deceleration using information about the driving environment and with the expectation that the human driver performs all remaining aspects of the Dynamic Driving Task. Level 2 Driving Automation The driving mode specific sustained performance by an ADS of all aspects of the Dynamic Driving Task within a given ODD with the expectation that the human driver will respond appropriately to a request to intervene. Level 3 System The driving mode specific sustained performance by an ADS of all aspects of the Dynamic Driving Task, even if a human driver does not respond appropriately to a request to intervene. Automated Driving System (ADS) Level 4 The full-time sustained performance by an ADS of all aspects of the Dynamic Driving Task under all roadway and environmental conditions that can be managed by a human driver. Level 5 *NOTE: Level 0 might include some ADAS features, but they are considered to be warning or momentary intervention systems at this level.

chunks.part: Part 9 Traffic Control For Bicycle Facilities
chunks.text: This Chapter provides an overview of foundational driving automation system (see definition in Section 5A.03) technology terminology, key principles, considerations for traffic control device selection, and topics for agencies to consider. The MUTCD does not address standardization of digital infrastructure, geometric road design, traffic control device maintenance levels, minimum pavement conditions, or other items that might be important for safe and effective operation of driving automation system technologies.

chunks.part: Part 9 Traffic Control For Bicycle Facilities
chunks.section_title: Overview of Automated Vehicles and Connected Vehicles
chunks.text: Driving automation system technology automates some or all aspects of the driving tasks to assist or replace the human driver and can include driver assistance technology generally known as advanced driver assistance systems (ADAS). Automated vehicles (AVs) are vehicles in which at least one element of vehicle control (such as steering, speed control, or braking) occurs without direct human driver input. AVs function by gathering information from a suite of sensors that can include, but are not limited to: A. Cameras, B. Radar, C. Light detection and ranging (LiDAR), D. Ultrasonic, and E. Infrared.

chunks.part: Part 9 Traffic Control For Bicycle Facilities
chunks.section_title: Traffic Control Device Design and Use Considerations
chunks.text: Agencies should adopt traffic control device maintenance policies and or practices with consideration to both the human driver and driving automation system technology needs (see Sections 1D.10, 2A.19, 3A.05 and 4A.10).

chunks.chapter: Chapter 5B. Provisions For Traffic Control Devices
chunks.text: Driving automation systems use sensors, algorithms, and processing to locate, read, and comprehend traffic signs and assist the human driver or AV in appropriately making vehicle operational decisions. Location, condition, uniformity, design characteristics, and consistent application all affect the ability of driving automation systems to perform these functions.

question: What A, B, and C advance-warning sign spacings does Table 6B-1 recommend for an expressway or freeway?
answer:
Direct Answer: For expressways and freeways, Table 6B-1 recommends placing the first advance warning sign (A) 1,000 feet from the transition area, the second sign (B) 1,500 feet beyond the first, and the third sign (C) 2,640 feet beyond the second. These distances are intended as guidance and should be adjusted based on engineering judgment and field conditions.

Guidance (recommended):
- The distances contained in Table 6B-1 are approximate, are intended for guidance purposes only, and should be applied with engineering judgment. These distances should be adjusted for field conditions, if necessary, by increasing or decreasing the recommended distances.
- On freeways and expressways, advance warning sign placement should extend as far as ½ mile or more because drivers are conditioned to uninterrupted flow.
- Where highway conditions permit, warning signs should be placed in advance of the transition and activity areas at varying distances depending on roadway type, condition, and posted speed. For freeways and expressways, the closest sign to the transition and activity areas should be placed approximately 1,000 feet or more.

Options (permitted):
- Because it is impracticable in mobile operations to redirect the road users’ normal path with stationary channelization, more dominant vehicle-mounted traffic control devices, such as arrow boards, portable changeable message signs, and high-intensity rotating, flashing, oscillating, or strobe lights, may be used instead of channelizing devices to establish a transition area.

chunks.text: Since rural highways are normally characterized by higher speeds, the effective placement of the first warning sign in feet should be substantially longer-from 8 to 12 times the speed limit in mph. chunks.text: On urban streets, the effective placement of the nearest warning sign to the TTC zone, in feet, should range from 4 to 8 times the speed limit in mph, with the high end of the range being used when speeds are relatively high. question: According to Table 6B-3, what taper lengths are used for shifting, shoulder, and one-lane two-way traffic tapers?
answer:
Direct Answer: According to Table 6B-3, a shifting taper should be at least 0.5 L, a shoulder taper should be at least 0.33 L, and a one-lane two-way traffic taper should be between 50 feet minimum and 100 feet maximum. These lengths are based on the calculated value L from Table 6B-4, except for the one-lane taper which uses fixed dimensions.

Guidance (recommended):
- A shifting taper should have a length of approximately ½ L (see Tables 6B-3 and 6B-4).
- If used, shoulder tapers should have a length of approximately ¹⁄3 L (see Tables 6B-3 and 6B-4).
- The appropriate taper length (L) should be determined using the criteria shown in Tables 6B-3 and 6B-4.
- A taper having a minimum length of 50 feet and a maximum length of 100 feet with channelizing devices at approximately 20-foot spacing should be used to guide traffic into the one-lane section, and a downstream taper should be used to guide traffic back into their original lane.

question: What minimum off-roadway sizes does Table 9A-1 give for a STOP sign, a YIELD sign, and a Crossbuck sign on a bicycle facility?
answer:
Direct Answer: For bicycle facilities, Table 9A-1 specifies that a STOP sign (R1-1) and a YIELD sign (R1-2) must each be at least 18 x 18 inches when installed off-roadway. The Crossbuck sign (R15-1), used at grade crossings on bicycle paths, has a minimum off-roadway size of 24 x 4.5 inches.

Standards (mandatory):
- The minimum sign and plaque sizes for signs specific to bicycle-only facilities and shared-use paths shall be those shown in Table 9A-1.
- STOP (R1-1) signs shall be installed on bicycle facilities at points where bicyclists are required to stop.
- YIELD (R1-2) signs shall be installed on bicycle facilities at points where bicyclists have an adequate view of conflicting traffic and are required to yield the right-of-way.

Guidance (recommended):
- Consideration should be given to selecting pavement marking materials that will minimize loss of traction for bicycles under wet conditions.

Options (permitted):
- Larger sizes of signs and plaques may be used on bicycle facilities when appropriate.
- Any diamond-shaped warning sign that is placed such that it is applicable only to bicyclists or pedestrians on shared-use paths or separated bicycle lanes may be 18" x 18".

Visual evidence:
[Image 1] Table 9A-1 (p.1036) lists the minimum off-roadway size for a Stop sign (R1-1) as 18 x 18 inches, for a Yield sign (R1-2) as 18 x 18 inches, and for a Grade Crossing (Crossbuck) sign (R15-1) as 24 x 4.5 inches.
[Image 2] Figure 9A-1 (p.1048) illustrates the minimum vertical clearance (4 ft) and lateral offset (2 ft) for post-mounted signs on shared-use paths.
[Image 6] Page 1049 shows Table 9A-1, Sheet 1 of 3, confirming the off-roadway minimum sizes for Stop, Yield, and Crossbuck signs.

Citations:
- Section 9A.02 Standard

chunks.part: Part 9 Traffic Control For Bicycle Facilities
chunks.chapter: Chapter 8E. Pathway And Sidewalk Grade Crossings
chunks.section_title: Passive Traffic Control Devices – Crossbuck Assemblies
chunks.text: The minimum height, measured vertically from the bottom of the YIELD or STOP sign to the elevation of the near edge of the pathway or sidewalk, of Crossbuck Assemblies installed on pathways or sidewalks shall be 4 feet where the lateral offset to the nearest edge of the sign is 2 feet or more and shall be 7 feet where the lateral offset to the nearest edge of the sign is less than 2 feet (see Figure 8E-5). * ** Mounting height shall be at least 7 feet for sidewalks where the lateral offset is less than 2 feet, at least 4 feet for sidewalks where the lateral offset is 2 feet or more, and at least 4 feet for pathways. Measured to the elevation at the near edge of the pathway or sidewalk. Notes: YIELD or STOP signs are used only at passive crossings. A STOP sign is used only if an engineering study determines that it is appropriate for that particular approach.

question: Which MUTCD table gives a fixed replacement interval, in years, for every type of traffic sign?
answer:
Direct Answer: The MUTCD does not provide a fixed replacement interval, in years, for every type of traffic sign. Instead, it specifies minimum maintained retroreflectivity levels and compliance dates for certain provisions, but no universal timetable for replacing signs based solely on age.

Standards (mandatory):
- None of the provided evidence contains a Standard provision mandating a fixed replacement interval in years for all traffic signs.

Guidance (recommended):
- None of the provided evidence contains a Guidance provision recommending a fixed replacement interval in years for all traffic signs.

Options (permitted):
- None of the provided evidence contains an Option provision permitting a fixed replacement interval in years for all traffic signs.

Visual evidence:
- [Image 1] Table 2D-2 provides recommended minimum letter and numeral sizes for guide signs based on speed and mounting, not replacement intervals.
- [Image 2] Figure 6B-1 illustrates the component parts of a temporary traffic control zone, not sign replacement schedules.
- [Image 3] Table 6B-1 shows recommended advance warning sign spacing distances by road type, not replacement intervals.

chunks.text: Many of the provisions in this Manual that are explicitly prohibitive have been included to address practices that have been shown to be ineffective, unsafe, or inconsistent with uniformity. The absence of a provision in this Manual that explicitly prohibits a particular practice, use, design, application, operation, or other aspect of a traffic control device does not, in itself, constitute acceptability or permission to use the device in a manner not provided for in this Manual. question: What crash modification factor for installing an ALL-WAY plaque is listed in Table 2B-1?
answer:
Direct Answer: The provided evidence does not list any crash modification factor for installing an ALL-WAY plaque in Table 2B-1. Table 2B-1, as shown, contains only regulatory sign and plaque sizes, not safety performance data or crash modification factors.

Standards (mandatory):
- At intersections where all approaches are controlled by STOP signs, an ALL-WAY (R1-3P) supplemental plaque shall be mounted below each STOP sign, with a white legend and border on a red background.

Options (permitted):
- The EXCEPT RIGHT TURN (R1-10P) plaque may be mounted below the STOP sign if an engineering study determines that a special combination of geometry and traffic volumes allows right-turning traffic to enter the intersection without stopping.

Visual evidence:
[Image 1] Figure 2B-1 shows the design and placement of the STOP sign (R1-1), YIELD sign (R1-2), and associated plaques including the ALL-WAY (R1-3P) plaque.

[Image 2] Page 68 shows Table 2B-1, which lists regulatory sign and plaque sizes for different road types, but does not include crash modification factors.

- The colors to be used on signs and their specific uses shall be as provided in the applicable Sections of this Manual. The color coordinates and values shall be as described in 23 CFR, Part 655, Subpart F, Appendix.

chunks.part: Part 9 Traffic Control For Bicycle Facilities
chunks.section_title: Traffic Control Device Design and Use Considerations
chunks.text: The interaction of traffic control devices with driving automation systems can create many challenges for agencies in determining traffic control device selection and application. The lack of tolerance of driving automation systems for non-uniformity in traffic control device design and application is a limiting factor of current driving automation system sophistication. This is because driving automation systems have a limited ability to interpolate across gaps in traffic control device cues to the vehicle in the following types of situations: A. The driving automation system technology’s ability to adapt to existing traffic control device design and typical quality, such as the refresh rates of electronic changeable message sign displays or the overall quality of a device that has been in service on the roadway for many years; B. The color perception of signs; C. The electronically perceptible conspicuity and contrast of markings in different environments and lighting conditions; D. The driving automation system camera technology and device photometric characteristics in interpreting various types of traffic signals E. The ability to discern and comprehend temporary traffic control devices and their varying applications, such as active electronic display devices or flaggers; and F. The ability to decipher traffic control at highway-rail or highway-LRT grade crossings, especially at passive grade crossings.

question: Which table lists State-by-State monetary fines for violating a No Turn on Red sign?
answer:
Direct Answer: The MUTCD does not contain a table listing State-by-State monetary fines for violating a No Turn on Red sign. It provides guidance on using higher fines zone signs in work zones and shows examples of fine-related plaques, but it does not specify or tabulate actual dollar amounts by state.

Standards (mandatory):
- Where a right turn on a circular red signal indication is to be prohibited, a NO TURN ON RED (R10-11, R10-11b) word message sign shall be used.
- A NO TURN ON RED (symbolic circular red) (R10-11a) sign shall be used when the approach is controlled by both circular red and red arrow indications.
- If a pre-signal is installed upstream from a signalized intersection, a No Turn on Red sign shall be installed at the pre-signal for the approach that crosses the track if turns on red would otherwise be permitted at the downstream intersection.

Guidance (recommended):
- A BEGIN HIGHER FINES ZONE (R2-10) sign should be installed at or near the beginning of a TTC zone where increased fines are imposed for traffic violations, and an END HIGHER FINES ZONE (R2-11) sign should be installed at or near the downstream end of the TTC zone.
- A No Turn on Red sign should be considered when an engineering study finds conditions such as inadequate sight distance, unexpected conflicts, exclusive pedestrian phases, unacceptable pedestrian conflicts, more than three crashes in 12 months, or skew angles creating visibility difficulty.

Options (permitted):
- A WORK ZONE (G20-5aP) plaque may be mounted above a Speed Limit sign to emphasize a reduced speed limit in a TTC zone.
- An END WORK ZONE SPEED LIMIT (R2-12) sign may be installed at the downstream end of the reduced speed limit zone.

chunks.chapter: Chapter 2B. Regulatory Signs, Barricades, And Gates
chunks.section_title: No Turn on Red Signs (R10-11 Series, R10-17a, and R10-30)
chunks.text: A No Turn on Red sign should be considered when an engineering study finds that one or more of the following conditions exists: A. Inadequate sight distance to vehicles approaching from the left (or right, if applicable); B. Geometrics or operational characteristics of the intersection that might result in unexpected conflicts; C. An exclusive pedestrian or bicycle phase; D. An unacceptable number of conflicting pedestrian movements with right-turn-on-red maneuvers, especially involving children, older pedestrians, or persons with disabilities; E. More than three right-turn-on-red crashes reported in a 12-month period for the particular approach; or F. The skew angle of the intersecting roadways creates difficulty for drivers to see traffic approaching from their left (or right, if applicable).

question: What manufacturer warranty periods are listed in Table 2A-5 for each retroreflective sheeting type?
answer:
Direct Answer: Table 2A-5 in the MUTCD lists minimum maintained retroreflectivity levels for different sign colors and sheeting types, but it does not specify any manufacturer warranty periods for those sheeting types. The table focuses on performance metrics, not product warranties.

Standards (mandatory):
- Public agencies or officials having jurisdiction shall use an assessment or management method designed to maintain sign retroreflectivity at or above the minimum levels in Table 2A-5.

Guidance (recommended):
- Except for signs identified in Section 2A.22 §5, one or more methods from “Maintaining Traffic Sign Retroreflectivity” (FHWA-SA-07-020, Revised 2013) or a method based on an engineering study should be used to maintain retroreflectivity at or above the levels in Table 2A-5; signs below those levels should be replaced.

Options (permitted):
- Highway agencies may exclude Parking, Standing, and Stopping (R7 and R8 series), Walking/Hitchhiking/Crossing (R9 series, R10-1 through R10-4b), Acknowledgment, and exclusive-use Bikeway signs from the retroreflectivity maintenance guidelines.

Visual evidence:
[Image 4] Table 2A-5 on page 63 shows minimum maintained retroreflectivity levels for various sign colors and sheeting types, including Beaded Sheeting Types I, II, III and Prismatic Sheeting, with no mention of warranty periods.

Citations:
- Section 2A.22 Standard §2 (p.62)
- Section 2A.22 Guidance §4 (p.62)
- Section 2A.22 Option §5 (p.63)
- Table 2A-5 (p.62)

question: In Figure 1B-1, what happens immediately after FHWA approves a request to experiment?
answer:
Direct Answer: Immediately after FHWA approves a request to experiment, the requesting jurisdiction installs the experimental traffic control device. The jurisdiction is then required to evaluate the device and provide semi-annual reports to FHWA.

Standards (mandatory):
- A traffic control device or application that does not comply with the provisions of this Manual shall not be used on any street, highway, bikeway, or site roadway open to public travel without first receiving official approval to experiment from the FHWA’s Office of Transportation Operations.

Guidance (recommended):
- Before requesting permission to experiment with a new device or application, an owner of a site roadway open to public travel should first check for any laws, regulations, and/or directives covering the application of the MUTCD that might apply.

Options (permitted):
- An agency may request a preliminary assessment of the viability of a potential request for experimentation by submitting an abstract that briefly describes the experimental concept.

Visual evidence:
[Image 1] Figure 1B-1 shows that immediately after “Approved?” is answered “Yes,” the next step is “Requesting jurisdiction installs experimental traffic control device.”
[Image 2] Page 7 confirms Figure 1B-1 depicts the process for requesting and conducting experimentations with traffic control devices.

question: In Figure 1B-2, if a proposed change is accepted for Federal rulemaking, what process follows before a Final Rule is published?
answer:
Direct Answer: If a proposed change is accepted for Federal rulemaking, the FHWA develops device provisions for inclusion in the next Notice of Proposed Amendments. This notice is then published in the Federal Register, followed by a public comment period. After reviewing comments, the FHWA prepares and publishes the Final Rule.

Standards (mandatory):
- None directly address the process after acceptance for rulemaking; the flowchart in Figure 1B-2 illustrates this as a procedural sequence without using “shall.”

Guidance (recommended):
- None explicitly recommend steps after acceptance for rulemaking; the process is depicted visually and described supportively.

Options (permitted):
- None permit alternative processes; the path shown is the established procedure.

Visual evidence:
[Image 5] Figure 1B-2 shows that after a change is accepted for Federal rulemaking, the FHWA develops device provisions for the next Notice of Proposed Amendments, which is published in the Federal Register, followed by a docket comment period, review of comments, preparation of a Final Rule, and publication of the Final Rule.

Citations:
- Section 1B.06 Support §4 (p.9)
- Section 1B.07 Support §3 (p.11)
- Figure 1B-2 (p.9)

question: In Figure 2A-2, what minimum mounting height and lateral offset are shown for a basic roadside sign in a rural area without a wider shoulder?
answer:
Direct Answer: For a basic roadside sign in a rural area without a wider shoulder, Figure 2A-2 shows a minimum mounting height of 5 feet from the bottom of the sign to the near edge of the pavement, and a minimum lateral offset of 12 feet from the edge of the traveled way. These dimensions are illustrated in diagram A of the figure.

Standards (mandatory):
- In rural areas, the minimum height, measured vertically from the bottom of the sign to the elevation of the near edge of the pavement, of signs installed at the side of the road shall be 5 feet (see Figure 2A-2).

Guidance (recommended):
- For post-mounted signs, the minimum lateral offset should be 12 feet from the edge of the traveled way. If a shoulder wider than 6 feet exists, the minimum lateral offset for post-mounted signs should be 6 feet from the edge of the shoulder.

Visual evidence:
- [Image 1] Figure 2A-2 (p.51) shows diagram A for a “Roadside sign in rural area” with a 5 ft MIN. mounting height and a 12 ft MIN. lateral offset from the edge of the traveled way.
- [Image 2] Page 51 displays Figure 2A-2, which includes diagram A showing the 5-foot minimum height and 12-foot minimum lateral offset for a rural roadside sign without a wider shoulder.

Citations:
- Section 2A.15 Standard §4 (p.58)
- Section 2A.16 Guidance §3 (p.60)
- Figure 2A-2 (p.51)

question: From Figure 2B-1, identify the shapes of the STOP and YIELD signs and the color scheme of the ALL-WAY plaque.
answer:
Direct Answer: The STOP sign is octagonal and the YIELD sign is a downward-pointing triangle, both shown in Figure 2B-1. The ALL-WAY plaque has a white legend and border on a red background, as required by MUTCD standards.

Standards (mandatory):
- When it is determined that a full stop is always required on an approach to an intersection, a STOP (R1-1) sign (see Figure 2B-1) shall be used.
- The YIELD (R1-2) sign (see Figure 2B-1) shall not be displayed using a changeable message sign.
- At intersections where all approaches are controlled by STOP signs, an ALL-WAY (R1-3P) supplemental plaque (see Figure 2B-1) shall be mounted below each STOP sign. The ALL-WAY plaque shall have a white legend and border on a red background.

Visual evidence:
[Image 1] Figure 2B-1 shows the STOP sign (R1-1) as an octagon and the YIELD sign (R1-2) as an inverted triangle; the ALL-WAY plaque (R1-3P) is rectangular with a red background, white legend, and white border.

Citations:
- Section 2B.04 Standard §1 (p.74)
- Section 2B.05 Standard §2 (p.75)
- Section 2B.04 Standard §4 (p.74)
- Figure 2B-1 (p.74)

question: In the unsignalized midblock-crosswalk example in Figure 3B-16, how far in advance of the crosswalk are the yield lines shown?
answer:
Direct Answer: In the unsignalized midblock crosswalk example shown in Figure 3B-16, the yield lines are depicted as being placed 20 to 50 feet in advance of the nearest edge of the crosswalk. This distance is also recommended in the MUTCD text for placing Yield Here to Pedestrians signs when used with yield lines at such locations.

Guidance (recommended):
- If yield (stop) lines and Yield Here to (Stop Here for) Pedestrians signs are used in advance of a crosswalk that crosses an uncontrolled multi-lane approach, the signs should be placed 20 to 50 feet in advance of the nearest edge of the crosswalk (see Section 3B.19 and Figure 3B-16).

Visual evidence:
- [Image 1] Figure 3B-16 shows a diagram labeled “B – Unsignalized midblock crosswalk” with a dimensioned arrow indicating the yield line is placed “20 to 50 ft” in advance of the crosswalk.
- [Image 2] Page 574 displays Figure 3B-16, confirming the layout and the “20 to 50 ft” dimension for the unsignalized midblock crosswalk example.

Citations:
- Section 2B.19 Guidance §3 (p.81)
- Figure 3B-16 (p.574)

question: Name two optional pavement-marking features explicitly labeled in Figure 3D-1 at the roundabout.
answer:
Direct Answer: Figure 3D-1 explicitly labels two optional pavement-marking features at the roundabout: “Optional white diagonal markings” and a “Wide dotted white extension of circulatory roadway edge line.” These are shown as discretionary elements in the diagram.

Options (permitted):
- YIELD (word) and YIELD AHEAD (symbol or word) pavement markings may be used on approaches to roundabouts.
- A yellow edge line may be placed around the inner (left-hand) edge of the circulatory roadway and may be used to channelize traffic.
- Channelizing lines and chevron and diagonal markings may be used on the approaches to and within the circulatory roadway of multi-lane roundabouts to separate traffic lanes, discourage lane changing, and/or compensate for off-tracking of larger trucks and vehicles.

question: According to Figure 4D-2, what are the general minimum and maximum longitudinal distances from the stop line for the primary signal faces, absent the near-side supplemental-face exception?
answer:
Direct Answer: According to Figure 4D-2 and the accompanying text, primary signal faces must be located no less than 40 feet beyond the stop line. The maximum distance is 180 feet for 12-inch signal faces (or 8-inch faces used under an option), unless a near-side supplemental face is provided.

Standards (mandatory):
- A signal face installed to satisfy the requirements for primary left-turn and right-turn signal faces, and at least one and preferably both of the minimum of two primary signal faces required for the through movement on the approach, shall be located no less than 40 feet beyond the stop line, and no more than 180 feet beyond the stop line unless a supplemental near-side signal face is provided.
- The primary signal faces that are used to satisfy the longitudinal placement requirement shall simultaneously satisfy the lateral placement requirement described in Section 4D.07 (see Figure 4D-2).

Visual evidence:
[Image 1] Figure 4D-2 shows the longitudinal location of primary signal faces with a minimum distance of 40 feet from the stop line and a maximum of 180 feet for 12-inch signal faces (unless a near-side supplemental face is used).
[Image 2] Page 672 displays Figure 4D-2 with the same longitudinal distances marked: 40 ft minimum, 180 ft maximum for 12-inch faces without a near-side supplemental face.

Citations:
- Section 4D.08 Standard §1 (p.673)
- Figure 4D-2 (p.672)

question: What is the order of the pedestrian intervals shown in Figure 4I-4, and what minimum durations are labeled for the first and last intervals?
answer:
Direct Answer: Figure 4I-4 shows the pedestrian intervals in this order: Walk Interval, Pedestrian Change Interval, and Buffer Interval. The first interval (Walk) has a minimum labeled duration of 7 seconds, and the last interval (Buffer) has a minimum labeled duration of 2 seconds.

Standards (mandatory):
- A pedestrian change interval consisting of a flashing UPRAISED HAND (symbolizing DONT WALK) signal indication shall begin immediately following the WALKING PERSON (symbolizing WALK) signal indication. Following the pedestrian change interval, a buffer interval consisting of a steady UPRAISED HAND (symbolizing DONT WALK) signal indication shall be displayed for at least 2 seconds prior to the release of any conflicting vehicular movement.

Guidance (recommended):
- At locations where a leading pedestrian interval is used, the minimum time for the WALKING PERSON (symbolizing WALK) indication should be the time provided for the leading pedestrian interval plus 7 seconds.
- If a leading pedestrian interval is used, it should be at least 3 seconds in duration and should be timed to allow pedestrians to cross at least one lane of traffic or, in the case of a large corner radius, to travel far enough for pedestrians to establish their position ahead of the turning traffic before the turning traffic is released.

Options (permitted):
- The additional time provided by an extended push button press to satisfy pedestrian clearance time needs may be added to either the walk interval or the pedestrian change interval. The countdown display is optional for Pedestrian Change Intervals of 7 seconds or less. The Walk Interval may be reduced under some conditions.

Visual evidence:
- [Image 1] Figure 4I-4 shows the sequence of pedestrian intervals as Walk Interval, Pedestrian Change Interval, and Buffer Interval, with labels indicating a minimum of 7 seconds for the Walk Interval and 2 seconds for the Buffer Interval.
- [Image 2] Page 724 contains Figure 4I-4 and its supporting text, confirming the structure and timing of the intervals shown in the figure.
- [Image 5] Page TC-32 lists Figure 4I-4 as “Pedestrian Intervals” on page 724, confirming its location and title.

Citations:
- Section 4I.06 Standard §

question: List the six states shown in the sequence for a pedestrian hybrid beacon in Figure 4J-3.
answer:
Direct Answer: The six states shown in the sequence for a pedestrian hybrid beacon in Figure 4J-3 are: 1) Dark Until Activated, 2) Flashing Yellow Upon Activation, 3) Steady Yellow, 4) Steady Red During Pedestrian Walk Interval, 5) Alternating Flashing Red During Pedestrian Change Interval, and 6) Dark Again Until Activated. This sequence is mandated by the MUTCD for operation following pedestrian actuation.

Standards (mandatory):
- Following an actuation by a pedestrian, a pedestrian hybrid beacon face shall display a flashing CIRCULAR yellow signal indication, followed by a steady CIRCULAR yellow signal indication, followed by both steady CIRCULAR RED signal indications during the pedestrian walk interval, followed by alternating flashing CIRCULAR RED signal indications during the pedestrian change interval (see Figure 4J-3). Upon termination of the pedestrian change interval, the pedestrian hybrid beacon faces shall revert to a dark (not illuminated) condition.

Guidance (recommended):
- When an engineering study finds that installation of a pedestrian hybrid beacon is justified, then parking and other sight obstructions should be prohibited for at least 100 feet in advance of and at least 20 feet beyond the marked crosswalk, or site accommodations should be made through curb extensions or other techniques to provide adequate sight distance; and if installed within a signal system, the pedestrian hybrid beacon should be coordinated.

Options (permitted):
- An optional steady red clearance interval may be added after Interval 3, and an optional short buffer interval (alternating flashing red while the pedestrian signal heads are displaying a steady UPRAISED HAND) may be added after Interval 5.

Visual evidence:
[Image 1] Figure 4J-3 shows the six sequential states of a pedestrian hybrid beacon: 1. Dark Until Activated, 2. Flashing Yellow Upon Activation, 3. Steady Yellow, 4. Steady Red During Pedestrian Walk Interval, 5. Alternating Flashing Red During Pedestrian Change Interval, and 6. Dark Again Until Activated.
[Image 3] Page 729 displays Figure 4J-3 with the same six labeled states and legend defining SY, FY, SR, and FR signal indications.

Citations:
- Section 4J

question: What four main areas of a temporary traffic control zone are shown in Figure 6B-1, in order of travel?
answer:
Direct Answer: Figure 6B-1 shows the four main areas of a temporary traffic control zone in the order road users encounter them: the advance warning area, then the transition area, followed by the activity area, and finally the termination area. These areas are described in Sections 6B.04 through 6B.07.

Standards (mandatory):
- Except for mobile operations, when redirection of the road users’ normal path is required, road users shall be directed from the normal path to a new path with appropriate channelizing devices, traffic control devices, and/or TTC methods.

Guidance (recommended):
- Typical distances for placement of advance warning signs on freeways and expressways should be longer because drivers are conditioned to uninterrupted flow; therefore, the advance warning sign placement should extend on these facilities as far as ½ mile or more.
- On urban streets, the effective placement of the nearest warning sign to the TTC zone, in feet, should range from 4 to 8 times the speed limit in mph, with the high end of the range being used when speeds are relatively high.
- Since rural highways are normally characterized by higher speeds, the effective placement of the first warning sign in feet should be substantially longer—from 8 to 12 times the speed limit in mph.
- The distances contained in Table 6B-1 are approximate, are intended for guidance purposes only, and should be applied with engineering judgment; these distances should be adjusted for field conditions, if necessary, by increasing or decreasing the recommended distances.

Options (permitted):
- The advance warning area may vary from a single sign or high-intensity rotating, flashing, oscillating, or strobe lights on a vehicle to a series of signs in advance of the TTC zone activity area.
- When a single advance warning sign is used (in cases such as low-speed residential streets), the advance warning area may be as short as 100 feet.
- Advance warning may be eliminated when the activity area is sufficiently removed from the road users’ path so that it does not interfere with the normal flow.
- Because it is impracticable in mobile operations to redirect the road users’ normal path with stationary channelization, more dominant vehicle-mounted traffic control devices, such as arrow boards, portable changeable message signs, and high-intensity rotating, flashing, oscillating, or strobe

question: In Figure 6D-1, how is the preferred STOP/SLOW paddle positioned to stop traffic?
answer:
Direct Answer: To stop traffic, the flagger must face oncoming drivers and hold the STOP side of the paddle stationary with their arm extended horizontally away from their body. Their free hand should be raised with the palm facing traffic, above shoulder level. This position is shown in Figure 6D-1.

Standards (mandatory):
- To stop road users, the flagger shall face road users and aim the STOP paddle face toward road users in a stationary position with the arm extended horizontally away from the body. The free arm shall be held with the palm of the hand above shoulder level toward approaching traffic.

Guidance (recommended):
- The STOP/SLOW paddle should be the primary and preferred hand-signaling device because it gives road users more positive guidance than red flags.

Options (permitted):
- The STOP/SLOW paddle may be modified to improve conspicuity by incorporating either white or red flashing lights on the STOP face, and either white or yellow flashing lights on the SLOW face, arranged in specific patterns.

question: What is the principal layout difference between the pathway grade crossing and the sidewalk grade crossing in Figure 8E-1?
answer:
Direct Answer: The principal layout difference is that a pathway grade crossing exists in its own separate right-of-way, physically independent of any roadway, while a sidewalk grade crossing runs parallel to and within the highway right-of-way, close enough to the roadway that traffic control devices for the roadway can influence or warn sidewalk users. Pathways are typically used by both pedestrians and bicyclists, whereas sidewalks are usually for pedestrians only.

Standards (mandatory):
- Detectable warnings shall be used at pathway grade crossings where pedestrian travel is permitted and at sidewalk grade crossings and shall extend across the full width of the pathway or sidewalk.

Guidance (recommended):
- If used at a pathway or sidewalk grade crossing, the gate configuration, which might include a combination of automatic pedestrian gates and swing gates, should provide for full-width coverage of the pathway or sidewalk on each approach to the crossing.

Visual evidence:
[Image 1] Figure 8E-1 visually contrasts a pathway grade crossing (A), which lies in its own right-of-way separated from the railroad, with a sidewalk grade crossing (B), which is adjacent to and within the highway right-of-way next to the roadway.
[Image 2] Page 1035 contains Section 8E.01 §4, which explains that Figure 8E-1 illustrates the difference between a pathway grade crossing and a sidewalk grade crossing, noting the pathway’s independent alignment and physical separation from roadways versus the sidewalk’s proximity to the roadway within the highway right-of-way.

Citations:
- Section 8E.01 Support §4 (p.1035)
- Section 8E.04 Standard §7 (p.1038)
- Section 8E.09 Guidance §8 (p.1044)
- Figure 8E-1 (p.1035)

chunks.part: Part 9 Traffic Control For Bicycle Facilities
chunks.chapter: Chapter 8E. Pathway And Sidewalk Grade Crossings
chunks.text: Figure 8E-1 illustrates the difference between a pathway grade crossing and a sidewalk grade crossing. A pathway is frequently placed in its own right-of-way on an alignment that is independent of any roadway. If a pathway is built parallel to a roadway, it is physically separated from the roadway by an open space or barrier such that the traffic control devices for the roadway grade crossing do not exert an influence over or provide adequate warning to pathway users. A sidewalk runs parallel to a roadway within the highway right-of-way and is close enough to the edge of the roadway’s traveled way that the traffic control devices for the roadway grade crossing can frequently exert an influence over or provide adequate warning to sidewalk users. Pathways are typically used by both pedestrians and bicyclists, whereas sidewalks are typically used only by pedestrians.

question: What exact candela output is represented by each LED dot around the STOP sign in Figure 2A-1?
answer:
Direct Answer: The MUTCD does not specify the exact candela output for each LED dot around the STOP sign in Figure 2A-1. It only provides standards for flash rate, color, placement, and maximum diameter (¼ inch), but no photometric values such as candela are given.

Standards (mandatory):
- If flashed, all LED units shall flash simultaneously at a steady rate between 50 and 60 times per minute.
- All the LED units in a sign legend or border shall be illuminated simultaneously with no sequential (chasing) or variable flash rates (dancing), except as otherwise allowed in this Manual.
- A cluster of LEDs shall not be used within the border of a sign.
- The LEDs shall not protrude outside the sign border or legend, shall have a maximum diameter of ¼ inch, and shall be white or red for STOP signs.

Options (permitted):
- For STOP signs, LEDs may be placed within the border or within one border width within the background of the sign.

Visual evidence:
[Image 1] Figure 2A-1 (p.48) illustrates LEDs in the border of a STOP sign as one example of enhanced conspicuity, but provides no photometric data.
[Image 3] Page 746 and [Image 5] Page 726 contain unrelated signal face diagrams and do not address LED candela output.

Citations:
- Section 2A.12 Standard §10 (p.50)
- Section 2A.12 Standard §09 (p.50)
- Section 2A.12 Option §16 (p.50)
- Figure 2A-1 (p.48)
- Page 746
- Page 726

question: How many milliseconds does each steady-yellow and steady-red stage last in Figure 4J-3?
answer:
Direct Answer: The MUTCD does not specify the duration of the steady-yellow or steady-red stages in Figure 4J-3 in milliseconds. It provides recommended time ranges in seconds for the steady yellow change interval (3 to 6 seconds) and permits a steady red clearance interval, but no exact timing is mandated for these phases in the context of pedestrian hybrid beacons.

Standards (mandatory):
- Following an actuation by a pedestrian, a pedestrian hybrid beacon face shall display a flashing CIRCULAR yellow signal indication, followed by a steady CIRCULAR yellow signal indication, followed by both steady CIRCULAR RED signal indications during the pedestrian walk interval, followed by alternating flashing CIRCULAR RED signal indications during the pedestrian change interval (see Figure 4J-3).

Guidance (recommended):
- A steady yellow change interval should have a minimum duration of 3 seconds and a maximum duration of 6 seconds (see Section 4F.17). The longer intervals should be reserved for use on approaches with higher speeds.
- The steadily illuminated CIRCULAR YELLOW change interval should have a duration of at least 5 seconds, unless a different duration, within the range of durations recommended by Section 4F.17, is justified by engineering judgment.
- The minimum duration of the yellow change interval of a bicycle signal phase should be 3 seconds.

Options (permitted):
- A steady red clearance interval may be used after the steady yellow change interval.

Visual evidence:
[Image 1] Figure 4J-3 illustrates the sequence of signal indications for a pedestrian hybrid beacon, including steady yellow (SY) and steady red (SR) stages, but does not specify their duration in milliseconds or seconds.

Citations:
- Section 4J.03 Standard §2 (p.730)
- Section 4J.03 Guidance §11 (p.730)
- Section 6L.04 Guidance §10 (p.830)
- Section 4H.11 Guidance §2 (p.717)
- Section 4J.03 Option §12 (p.730)
- Figure 4J-3 (p.729)

question: What crash-reduction percentage is attributed to the bicycle box in Figure 9E-12?
answer:
Direct Answer: The MUTCD does not provide any specific crash-reduction percentage attributed to the bicycle box shown in Figure 9E-12. The manual describes how to install and use bicycle boxes but does not quantify their safety effectiveness with a percentage.

Standards (mandatory):
- If used, the distance from the upstream edge of the bicycle box that is nearest to the stop line for motor vehicles to the downstream edge of the bicycle box that is nearest the crosswalk or intersection shall be at least 10 feet. At least one bicycle symbol marking shall be used in the bicycle box.
- If used, green-colored pavement shall be used in the full limits of the bicycle box.

Guidance (recommended):
- Providing a bicycle box on a signalized intersection approach where a discernible number of conflicts between vehicles turning across through bicycles in a bicycle lane has been demonstrated during the green interval of a signal should be evaluated based on engineering judgment or study.
- A bicycle lane should be used on the approach to a bicycle box.
- A bicycle box should not be contiguous with a crosswalk.
- A stop line on the downstream end of the bicycle box should be used to mark the location where bicycles are required to stop.
- Countdown pedestrian signals for the crosswalk or pedestrian crossing movement that crosses the approach should accompany single-lane bicycle boxes where it is demonstrated that bicycles arrive at the intersection at or near the end of the red signal indication being displayed to traffic in the approach lane(s) that is behind the box.

Options (permitted):
- A bicycle box may be used to increase the visibility of stopped bicycles on the approach to a signalized intersection during the portion of the signal cycle when a red signal indication is being displayed to motor vehicles in the approach lane(s) that is behind the box.
- Green-colored pavement may be used in a bicycle box.

Visual evidence:
[Image 1] Figure 9E-12 shows examples of intersection bicycle boxes, including dimensions and optional green-colored pavement.
[Image 4] Page 1106 displays Figure 9E-12 (Sheet 1 of 2), illustrating a bicycle box across one lane with an advance stop line and associated signage.
[Image 3] Page 1107 displays Figure 9E-12 (Sheet 2 of 2), illustrating a bicycle box across multiple lanes

question: A provision appears under a Guidance heading and uses the word 'should.' Is it mandatory, and when may a deviation be appropriate?
answer:
Direct Answer: A provision under a Guidance heading using the word “should” is not mandatory. Deviations are allowed if engineering judgment or an engineering study indicates the deviation is appropriate for the specific conditions.

Standards (mandatory):
- Guidance statements are defined as recommended practice in typical situations, with deviations allowed if engineering judgment or engineering study indicates the deviation to be appropriate; the verb “should” is typically used in Guidance statements, and “shall” and “may” are not used in them.
- Standard statements are mandatory and use the verb “shall”; Guidance statements are labeled and appear in unbold italic type.

Guidance (recommended):
- Guide signs should be limited to no more than three lines of destinations, unless otherwise provided, and further minimized when multiple signs are in the same overhead display; distance messages or action information should be provided where appropriate.
- On conventional roads, guide signs for preferential lanes are ordinarily not needed, but if used, they should comply with Chapter 2D provisions and any applicable principles from Sections 2G.10 through 2G.15 that engineering judgment finds appropriate.

Options (permitted):
(none)

Visual evidence:
(none)

Citations:
- Section 1C.01 Standard §1 (p.13)
- Section 2D.06 Guidance §2 (p.209)
- Section 2G.10 Guidance §2 (p.420)

chunks.part: Part 9 Traffic Control For Bicycle Facilities
chunks.chapter: Chapter 1C. Definitions, Acronyms, And Abbreviations Used In This Manual
chunks.section_title: Definitions of Headings Used in this Manual
chunks.text: When used in this Manual, the text headings of Standard, Guidance, Option, and Support shall be defined as follows: A. Standard-a statement of required, mandatory, or specifically prohibitive practice regarding a traffic control device. In limited, location-specific cases, the results of a documented engineering study (see Section 1D.03) might indicate a deviation from one or more requirements of a Standard provision to be appropriate. All Standard statements are labeled, and the text appears in bold type. The verb “shall” is typically used. The verbs “should” and “may” are not used in Standard statements. Standard statements are sometimes modified by Option statements. B. Guidance-a statement of recommended practice in typical situations, with deviations allowed if engineering judgment or engineering study (see Section 1D.03) indicates the deviation to be appropriate. All Guidance statements are labeled, and the text appears in unbold italic type. The verb “should” is typically used. The verbs “shall” and “may” are not used in Guidance statements. Guidance statements are sometimes modified by Option statements. C. Option-a statement of practice that is a permissive condition and carries no requirement or recommendation. Option statements sometimes contain allowable modifications to a Standard or Guidance statement. All Option statements are labeled, and the text appears in unbold type. The verb “may” is typically used. The verbs “shall” and “should” are not used in Option statements. D. Support-an informational statement that does not convey any degree of mandate, recommendation, authorization, prohibition, or enforceable condition. Support statements are labeled, and the text appears in unbold type. The verbs “shall,” “should,” and “may” are not used in Support statements.

chunks.part: Part 9 Traffic Control For Bicycle Facilities
chunks.chapter: Chapter 1D. Provisions Applicable To Traffic Control Devices In General
chunks.text: The application of engineering study and engineering judgment is a fundamental principle of the use of traffic control devices. It is for this reason that, in most cases, the selection of a particular device is not required by a Standard provision, but is determined by engineering study or engineering judgment. Many Standard provisions in this Manual specifically require, by explicit language in the individual provisions or by implication, the application of engineering study or engineering judgment in applying those Standards. Site-specific conditions might result in the determination that it is impossible or impracticable to comply with a Standard at that location. In such a case, a deviation from the requirement of a particular Standard at that location might be the only possibility. In such limited, specific cases, the deviation is allowed, provided that the agency or official having jurisdiction fully documents, through an engineering study, the engineering basis for the deviation.

chunks.part: Part 9 Traffic Control For Bicycle Facilities
chunks.text: In general, the procedures illustrated represent minimum solutions for the situations depicted. Except for the notes (which are clearly classified using headings as being Standard, Guidance, Option, or Support), the information presented in the typical applications can generally be regarded as Guidance.

chunks.part: Part 9 Traffic Control For Bicycle Facilities
chunks.text: Except where otherwise provided in this Manual, guide signs should be limited to no more than three lines of destinations, which include place names, route numbers, street names, and cardinal directions. Where two or more signs are included in the same overhead display, the amount of legend should be further minimized. Where appropriate, a distance message or action information, such as an exit number, NEXT RIGHT, or directional arrows, should be provided on guide signs in addition to the destinations.

chunks.part: Part 9 Traffic Control For Bicycle Facilities
chunks.chapter: Chapter 1B. Legal Requirements For Traffic Control Devices
chunks.text: For the purposes of Paragraph 2 of this Section, policies, directives, specifications, standard drawings, or similar documents that are issued by an agency and that change or modify Standard, Guidance, or Option provisions in this Manual shall be considered as supplements to the MUTCD and shall also be revised to be in substantial conformance with the National MUTCD. question: Using Figure 2A-1 and Section 2A.11, describe the requirements for a retroreflective strip used on a sign support to enhance conspicuity.
answer:
Direct Answer: A retroreflective strip on a sign support must be at least 2 inches wide, run the full length from the sign to within 2 feet of the roadway edge, and match the sign’s background color—except for YIELD and DO NOT ENTER signs, which require a red strip. The strip must not display any legend or information.

Standards (mandatory):
- If a strip of retroreflective material is used on the sign support, it shall be at least 2 inches in width, it shall be placed for the full length of the support from the sign to within 2 feet above the near edge of the roadway, and its color shall match the background color of the sign, except that the color of the strip for the YIELD and DO NOT ENTER signs shall be red. The retroreflective strip shall not display any legend or other information.

Guidance (recommended):
(none)

Options (permitted):
(none)

Visual evidence:
[Image 1] Figure 2A-1 illustrates a vertical retroreflective strip on a sign support, extending from the sign down to within 2 feet of the roadway edge.
[Image 6] Figure 8B-2 shows a 2-inch white retroreflective strip on the back of a Crossbuck support and an optional 2-inch red or white strip on the front, both running from the sign to within 2 feet of the roadway edge.

Citations:
- Section 2A.11 Standard §5 (p.49)
- Figure 2A-1 (p.48)
- Figure 8B-2 (p.997)

chunks.text: Based upon engineering judgment, where the improvement of the conspicuity of a standard regulatory, warning, or guide sign is desired, any of the following methods may be used, as appropriate, to enhance the sign’s conspicuity (see Figure 2A-1): A. A legend of “NOTICE,” “STATE LAW,” or other appropriate text may be added in black letters within the header panel for a period of time determined by engineering judgment. D. Adding a NEW plaque (see Section 2C.60) above a new standard regulatory or warning sign, for a period of time in accordance with Paragraph 3 of this Section, to call attention to the new sign. Adding a Warning Beacon (see Section 4S.03) to a standard regulatory (other than a STOP, DO NOT ENTER, WRONG WAY, or a Speed Limit sign), warning, or guide sign. H. Adding light-emitting diode (LED) units within the symbol, legend, or border of a standard regulatory, warning, or guide sign, as provided in Section 2A.12. L. Adding a strip of retroreflective material to the sign support in accordance with the provisions of Paragraph 5 of this Section. M. Using other methods that are specifically allowed for certain signs as described elsewhere in this Manual.

question: For a basic rural roadside sign, combine Figure 2A-2 with Sections 2A.15 and 2A.16 to state the normal minimum mounting height and lateral offset.
answer:
Direct Answer: For a basic rural roadside sign, the normal minimum mounting height is 5 feet from the bottom of the sign to the near edge of the pavement. The normal minimum lateral offset is 12 feet from the edge of the traveled way, or 6 feet from the edge of the shoulder if one exists.

Standards (mandatory):
- In rural areas, the minimum height, measured vertically from the bottom of the sign to the elevation of the near edge of the pavement, of signs installed at the side of the road shall be 5 feet.
- For overhead sign supports, the minimum lateral offset from the edge of the shoulder (or if no shoulder exists, from the edge of the pavement) to the near edge of overhead sign supports (cantilever or sign bridges) shall be 6 feet.

Guidance (recommended):
- Signs should be individually installed on separate posts or mountings except where one sign supplements another.

Options (permitted):
- On conventional, low-volume rural, and special-purpose roads in areas where it is impractical to locate a sign with the lateral offset prescribed by this Section because of roadside features such as terrain or vegetation, a lateral offset of at least 2 feet may be used.

question: A portable CMS designer proposes 'DLY' to mean DELAY. Using Section 1D.08 and Table 1D-3, is this acceptable and why?
answer:
Direct Answer: No, using 'DLY' to mean DELAY on a portable CMS is not acceptable. The MUTCD explicitly prohibits this abbreviation in Table 1D-3 because it can be misinterpreted as "Daily," which could confuse drivers.

Standards (mandatory):
- The abbreviations shown in Table 1D-3 shall not be used in connection with traffic control devices because of their potential to be misinterpreted by road users.
- Abbreviations displayed on CMS shall comply with the provisions of Section 1D.08.

Visual evidence:
[Image 1] Table 1D-3 lists 'DLY' under "Abbreviation" with "Delay" as the "Intended Word" and "Daily" as the "Common Misinterpretation," indicating it is unacceptable.
[Image 3] Page 37 shows Table 1D-3 titled “Unacceptable Abbreviations,” confirming 'DLY' is prohibited.

Citations:
- Section 2L.05 Standard §6 (p.516)
- Section 1D.08 Standard §4 (p.34)
- Table 1D-3 (p.37)

question: At an all-way stop, what plaque arrangement and appearance are required by Section 2B.04 and Figure 2B-1, and may a 4-WAY plaque be substituted?
answer:
Direct Answer: At an all-way stop, the MUTCD requires that an ALL-WAY (R1-3P) plaque be mounted below each STOP sign. This plaque must have a white legend and border on a red background. A 4-WAY plaque or any other numbered-way plaque is strictly prohibited.

Standards (mandatory):
- At intersections where all approaches are controlled by STOP signs, an ALL-WAY (R1-3P) supplemental plaque shall be mounted below each STOP sign. The ALL-WAY plaque shall have a white legend and border on a red background.
- Supplemental plaques with legends such as 2-WAY, 3-WAY, 4-WAY, or other numbers of ways shall not be used with STOP signs.

Visual evidence:
[Image 1] Figure 2B-1 shows the required appearance of the ALL-WAY (R1-3P) plaque as a rectangular sign with “ALL WAY” in white text on a red background, positioned below the STOP sign.
[Image 3] Page 74 displays Section 2B.04, which mandates the use of the ALL-WAY plaque at all-way stops and prohibits numbered-way plaques like 4-WAY.

Citations:
- Section 2B.04 Standard §4 (p.74)
- Section 2B.04 Standard §5 (p.74)
- Figure 2B-1 (p.74)

question: Compare the quantitative triggers in the four-leg All-Way Stop crash warrant and the 8-hour volume warrant.
answer:
Direct Answer: The four-leg All-Way Stop crash warrant requires five or more reportable crashes in 12 months (or six in 36 months), while the 8-hour volume warrant for all-way stop control requires at least 300 combined units per hour on major-street approaches and 200 on minor-street approaches for any 8 hours. These are separate warrants with different quantitative thresholds and purposes.

Standards (mandatory):
- None of the provided text contains Standard provisions comparing these two warrants.

Guidance (recommended):
- None of the provided text contains Guidance provisions comparing these two warrants.

Options (permitted):
- All-way stop control may be installed at a four-leg intersection where an engineering study indicates five or more reported crashes in 12 months (or six in 36 months) of a type correctable by all-way stop control.
- All-way stop control may be installed where an engineering study indicates combined motor vehicle, bicycle, and pedestrian volume is at least 300 units per hour on major-street approaches and 200 units per hour on minor-street approaches for any 8 hours of a typical day.

Citations:
- Section 2B.13 Option §1 (p.79)
- Section 2B.16 Option §1 (p.79)

question: If an agency is using an approved retroreflectivity-management method but a few individual signs temporarily fall below Table 2A-5, is the agency automatically out of compliance? Include the white-on-red thresholds relevant to STOP-type signs.
answer:
Direct Answer: No, an agency is not automatically out of compliance if a few individual signs temporarily fall below the minimum retroreflectivity levels in Table 2A-5, as long as it is actively using an approved assessment or management method. For white-on-red STOP-type signs, the minimum maintained retroreflectivity level is 50 cd/lx/m² for prismatic sheeting (Type III) and 15 cd/lx/m² for beaded sheeting (Type II), with a required contrast ratio of at least 3:1 between white and red.

Standards (mandatory):
- Public agencies or officials having jurisdiction shall use an assessment or management method that is designed to maintain sign retroreflectivity at or above the minimum levels in Table 2A-5.

Guidance (recommended):
- Except for those signs specifically identified in Paragraph 5 of this Section, one or more of the methods described in “Maintaining Traffic Sign Retroreflectivity,” (FHWA-SA-07-020, Revised 2013), FHWA, or a method developed based on an engineering study, should be used to maintain sign retroreflectivity at or above the minimum levels in Table 2A-5. Signs that are identified through the agency’s method as being below the minimum levels should be replaced.

Options (permitted):
- Highway agencies may exclude the following signs from the retroreflectivity maintenance guidelines described in this Section: A. Parking, Standing, and Stopping (R7 and R8 series) signs; B. Walking/Hitchhiking/Crossing (R9 series, R10-1 through R10-4b) signs; C. Acknowledgment signs; and D. Bikeway signs that are intended for exclusive use by bicyclists or pedestrians.

question: On a multi-lane roadway posted at 35 mph, may the single-lane regulatory-sign size be used, and what size must a STOP sign still use?
answer:
Direct Answer: On a multi-lane roadway posted at 35 mph, the single-lane regulatory-sign size may be used only if engineering judgment determines it is appropriate and the reduced legend size is adequate. However, a STOP sign must still use the standard size for its type, as its dimensions are not governed by the same speed-based tables as guide signs.

Standards (mandatory):
- The sign dimensions prescribed in the sign size tables in this Manual shall be used unless engineering judgment determines that other sizes are appropriate; where smaller sizes are used, they shall not be less than the minimum dimensions specified in this Manual.
- The sizes shown in the Minimum columns that are smaller than the sizes shown in the Conventional Road columns shall only be used on low-speed roadways, alleys, site roadways open to public travel, and on low-volume rural roads with operating speeds of 30 mph or less; and only where the reduced legend size would be adequate for the regulation or warning or where physical conditions preclude the use of larger sizes.

Guidance (recommended):
- For guide signs on multi-lane roadways, Table 2D-2 recommends using the “30–40 mph” column for letter and numeral sizes when the posted speed is 35 mph.

Options (permitted):
- Engineering judgment may determine that sign dimensions smaller than those prescribed in the tables are appropriate, provided they are not less than the minimum dimensions specified in the Manual.

Visual evidence:
[Image 1] Table 2D-2 provides recommended minimum letter and numeral sizes for conventional road guide signs based on speed and lane configuration, showing different sizes for single-lane versus multi-lane roadways.
[Image 5] Page 74 shows Section 2B.04, which establishes that the STOP sign (R1-1) shall be used when a full stop is always required, but does not specify size variations based on speed or lane count for the STOP sign itself.

Citations:
- Section 2A.07 Standard §2 (p.45)
- Section 2D.07 Guidance §5 (p.210)
- Table 2D-2 (p.210)

question: For a potential stop condition on a 55-mph approach, what advance placement distance is shown in Table 2C-3, and should it be treated as an inflexible mandatory distance?
answer:
Direct Answer: For a 55-mph approach, Table 2C-3 shows an advance placement distance of 990 feet for Condition A (potential stop situation). This distance is not mandatory; it is a guideline that should be adjusted using engineering judgment based on site conditions and visibility.

Standards (mandatory):
- The Stop Ahead (W3-1), Yield Ahead (W3-2), and Signal Ahead (W3-3) Advance Traffic Control signs shall be installed on an approach to a primary traffic control device that is not visible for a sufficient distance to permit the road user to respond to the device (see Table 2C-3).
- If a YIELD or STOP sign is present at a passive grade crossing, a Yield Ahead (W3-2) or Stop Ahead (W3-1) Advance Warning sign shall also be installed if the criteria for their installation given in Section 2C.35 is met. The Yield Ahead or Stop Ahead sign shall be located in accordance with Table 2C-3.

Guidance (recommended):
- Warning signs should be placed so that they provide an adequate PRT. The distances contained in Table 2C-3 should be applied with engineering judgment.
- The effectiveness of the placement of warning signs should be periodically evaluated under both day and night conditions.

Options (permitted):
- A NEXT XX MILES (W7-3aP) supplemental distance plaque may be installed below the Winding Road sign where continuous roadway curves exist for a specific distance.

question: For a curve with an advisory speed of 40 mph and a radius within 401 to 700 feet, what Chevron Alignment sign spacing and placement are indicated?
answer:
Direct Answer: For a curve with a 40 mph advisory speed and a radius between 401 and 700 feet, Chevron Alignment signs should be spaced 120 feet apart, measured from the point of curvature. These signs must be installed on the outside of the curve, in line with and at a right angle to approaching traffic, at a minimum height of 4 feet.

Standards (mandatory):
- Chevron Alignment signs shall be installed on the outside of a turn or curve, in line with and at approximately a right angle to approaching traffic. Chevron Alignment signs shall be installed at a minimum height of 4 feet, measured vertically from the bottom of the sign to the elevation of the near edge of the traveled way.

Guidance (recommended):
- The approximate spacing of Chevron Alignment signs on the turn or curve measured from the point of curvature (PC) should be as shown in Table 2C-5.

Options (permitted):
- LEDs may be used to enhance the conspicuity of Chevron Alignment signs.
- Chevron Alignment signs may be used instead of or in addition to standard delineators.

Visual evidence:
[Image 1] Table 2C-5 shows that for an advisory speed of 35 to 45 mph and a curve radius of 401 to 700 feet, the sign spacing is 120 feet.
[Image 2] Figure 2C-2 illustrates how Chevron Alignment signs (W1-8L and W1-8R) are placed along the outside of a curve, aligned with the direction of travel.
[Image 3] Page 158 displays Table 2C-5, which specifies 120 feet spacing for a 40 mph advisory speed and 401–700 ft radius.
[Image 4] Page 156 presents Figure 2C-2, showing the placement of Chevron signs along a curve with an advisory speed plaque.
[Image 5] Page 154 lists Chevron Alignment signs as one of several treatments that might be used for horizontal alignment changes.
[Image 6] Page 619 (Figure 3G-1) shows delineator placement on curves and notes that Chevron Alignment signs may be used instead of or in addition to standard delineators.

question: At a 55-mph curve, when must a no-passing zone be marked, and what happens if the next no-passing zone begins less than 400 feet later?
answer:
Direct Answer: At a 55-mph curve, no-passing zone markings must be used if the passing sight distance is less than 990 feet (as shown in Table 3B-1 for 55 mph). If the next no-passing zone begins less than 400 feet away, the zones should be connected by continuous markings.

Standards (mandatory):
- On roadways with center line markings, no-passing zone markings shall be used at horizontal or vertical curves where the passing sight distance is less than the minimum shown in Table 3B-1 for the 85th-percentile speed or the speed limit.
- On two-way, two-lane or three-lane roadways where center line markings are installed, no-passing zones shall be established at vertical and horizontal curves and other locations where an engineering study indicates that passing must be prohibited because of inadequate sight distances or other special conditions.
- No-passing zones shall be marked by either the one-direction no-passing zone pavement markings or the two-direction no-passing zone pavement markings described in Section 3B.01 and shown in Figures 3B-1 and 3B-3.

Guidance (recommended):
- Where the distance between successive no-passing zones is less than 400 feet, no-passing zone markings should connect the zones.

Citations:
- Section 3B.03 Standard §4 (p.543)
- Section 3B.03 Standard §3 (p.543)
- Section 3B.03 Standard §1 (p.542)
- Section 3B.03 Guidance §7 (p.543)

question: For Warrant 1 Condition A with at least two major-street lanes and one minor-street lane, what volumes must exist and over what time basis, and does meeting them compel signal installation?
answer:
Direct Answer: For Warrant 1 Condition A with at least two major-street lanes and one minor-street lane, the volumes must be measured over the same 8 hours for that condition. Meeting these volumes does not compel signal installation — it only means the need for a signal should be considered, based on an engineering study.

Standards (mandatory):
- The major-street and minor-street volumes for Condition A shall be for the same 8 hours; however, the 8 hours selected for Condition A analysis need not be the same as those for Condition B.
- The 8 hours satisfied in Condition A shall not be required to be the same 8 hours satisfied in Condition B.

Guidance (recommended):
- The need for a traffic control signal should be considered if an engineering study finds that the vehicles per hour given in both of the 100 percent columns of Condition A in Table 4C-1 exist on the major street and the more critical minor-street approach, respectively, for each of any 8 hours of an average day.
- The need for a traffic control signal should be considered if an engineering study finds that both of the following conditions exist for each of any 8 hours of an average day: (A) the vehicles per hour given in both of the 80 percent columns of Condition A in Table 4C-1 exist on the major street and the more critical minor-street approach, respectively; and (B) the vehicles per hour given in both of the 80 percent columns of Condition B in Table 4C-1 exist on the major street and the more critical minor-street approach, respectively.

Options (permitted):
- For signal warrants requiring conditions to be present for a certain number of hours, any four consecutive 15-minute periods may be considered as 1 hour, provided the separate 1-hour periods used in the warrant analysis do not overlap and both major-street and minor-street volumes are for the same specific 1-hour periods.

- Section 4C.02 Guidance §4 (p.653)
- Section 4C.02 Guidance §9 (p.654)

question: For a four-leg intersection evaluated under the one-year Crash Experience signal warrant, what crash thresholds apply and what two additional categories of conditions must also be satisfied?
answer:
Direct Answer: For a four-leg intersection under the one-year Crash Experience signal warrant, the crash thresholds are found in Table 4C-2 for either total angle and pedestrian crashes (all severities) or fatal-and-injury angle and pedestrian crashes. Two additional conditions must also be satisfied: an engineering study must show that alternative measures have failed to reduce crashes, and traffic volumes must meet the criteria in Table 4C-1 for at least 8 hours of an average day.

Standards (mandatory):
(none)

Guidance (recommended):
- The need for a traffic control signal should be considered if an engineering study finds that all of the following criteria are met: (A) adequate trial of alternatives with satisfactory observance and enforcement has failed to reduce the crash frequency; (B) at least one of the crash conditions in Table 4C-2 applies (either total angle/pedestrian crashes or fatal/injury angle/pedestrian crashes within 1 year); and (C) for each of any 8 hours of an average day, the vehicle volumes meet the thresholds in Table 4C-1.

Options (permitted):
- If the posted or statutory speed limit or the 85th-percentile speed on the major street exceeds 40 mph, or if the intersection lies within a built-up area of an isolated community with population under 10,000, agencies may use the 56 percent columns in Table 4C-1 instead of the 80 percent columns, and may substitute Tables 4C-4 and 4C-5 for Tables 4C-2 and 4C-3.
- Agencies may calibrate Highway Safety Manual safety performance functions or develop their own SPFs to produce agency-specific average crash frequency values, which may be used instead of those in Tables 4C-2 through 4C-5 when documented in the engineering study.

question: At an 85th-percentile approach speed of 45 mph, from how far in advance should the two primary signal faces be continuously visible, and what treatment is recommended if that view is unavailable?
answer:
Direct Answer: At an 85th-percentile speed of 45 mph, the two primary signal faces should be continuously visible from at least the minimum sight distance shown in Table 4D-2, measured to the stop line. If that visibility is not available due to obstructions or another signalized location, a warning sign should be installed to alert approaching traffic.

Guidance (recommended):
- The two primary signal faces should be continuously visible to approaching traffic from a point at least the minimum sight distance provided in Table 4D-2 in advance of and measured to the stop line, unless precluded by a physical obstruction or another signalized location within that range.
- If approaching traffic does not have a continuous view of at least two signal faces for at least the minimum sight distance shown in Table 4D-2, a sign should be installed to warn approaching traffic of the traffic control signal.
- For approaches with an 85th-percentile speed of 45 mph or higher, signal backplates should be used on all signal faces facing the approach, and supplemental pole-mounted or overhead signal faces should be considered to enhance visibility behind large vehicles.

question: Using Section 4I.06 and Figure 4I-4, describe the pedestrian interval order, minimum buffer interval, and walking speed normally used for clearance timing.
answer:
Direct Answer: The pedestrian interval sequence is Walk, then Pedestrian Change (flashing UPRAISED HAND), followed by a Buffer Interval (steady UPRAISED HAND). The minimum buffer interval is 2 seconds. A walking speed of 3.5 feet per second is normally used to calculate the required clearance time, though slower speeds may be considered for certain users.

Standards (mandatory):
- Following the pedestrian change interval, a buffer interval consisting of a steady UPRAISED HAND signal indication shall be displayed for at least 2 seconds prior to the release of any conflicting vehicular movement.
- The sum of the time of the pedestrian change interval and the buffer interval shall not be less than the calculated pedestrian clearance time.

Guidance (recommended):
- The pedestrian clearance time should be sufficient to allow a pedestrian who left the curb at the end of the WALK signal to travel at a walking speed of 3.5 feet per second to at least the far side of the traveled way or to a median of sufficient width.
- Where pedestrians who walk slower than 3.5 feet per second or use wheelchairs routinely use the crosswalk, a walking speed of less than 3.5 feet per second should be considered in determining the pedestrian clearance time.

Options (permitted):
- The additional time provided by an extended push button press to satisfy pedestrian clearance time needs may be added to either the walk interval or the pedestrian change interval.
- The countdown display is optional for Pedestrian Change Intervals of 7 seconds or less.
- The Walk Interval may be reduced under some conditions.

- [Image 1] Figure 4I-4 illustrates the sequence of pedestrian intervals: Walk, Pedestrian Change, and Buffer Interval, with a minimum 2-second buffer and a calculated clearance time based on walking speed.

- [Image 3] Page 723 provides context for pedestrian signal timing but does not detail the interval order or walking speed.
- [Image 4] Page 726 discusses leading pedestrian intervals but does not specify the standard clearance timing or walking speed.
